deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is Chapter 3 ('On the sum of the divisors of any number') of Euler's Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (E792). Euler writes ∫n for what is now σ(n), the sum of all divisors of n.

§86 (completed from the previous page). Let N have divisors 1, α, β, …, N, and let p be a prime not dividing N. The divisors of Np are the divisors d of N together with the products pd. The second group sums to p·σ(N). Hence
σ(Np) = σ(N) + pσ(N) = (p+1)σ(N) = σ(p)σ(N).

§87. In the same way, using §74 (the description of the divisors of Np² for p not dividing N), the divisors of Np² are d, pd and p²d. So
σ(Np²) = (1+p+p²)σ(N) = σ(N)σ(p²).
Likewise σ(Np³) = σ(N)σ(p³), and so on. In modern terms: if gcd(N,p)=1 then σ(Np^k) = σ(N)σ(p^k).

§88. Applying this to each 'class and species' of the previous chapter (a class is a number of divisors; a species is the shape of the factorisation), Euler lists:
- σ(p) = 1+p
- σ(p²) = 1+p+p²
- σ(pq) = (1+p)(1+q)
- σ(p³) = 1+p+p²+p³
- σ(p²q) = (1+p+p²)(1+q)
- σ(pqr) = (1+p)(1+q)(1+r)
- σ(p⁴) = 1+p+…+p⁴
- σ(p³q) = (1+p+p²+p³)(1+q)
- σ(p²q²) = (1+p+p²)(1+q+q²)
- σ(p²qr) = (1+p+p²)(1+q)(1+r)
- σ(pqrs) = (1+p)(1+q)(1+r)(1+s)
Here p, q, r, s are distinct primes.

§89. Recursions for prime powers:
- σ(p²) = p² + σ(p) = 1 + pσ(p)
- σ(p³) = p³ + σ(p²) = 1 + pσ(p²) = 1 + p + p²σ(p)
- σ(p⁴) and σ(p⁵) follow similarly.
In general:
σ(pⁿ) = 1 + pσ(p^{n−1}) = 1 + p + p²σ(p^{n−2}) = 1 + p + p² + p³σ(p^{n−3}) = …
Each follows from σ(pⁿ) = Σ_{k=0}^{n} p^k. Equivalently σ(pⁿ) = pⁿ + σ(p^{n−1}), which is the first form he writes for n=2,3.

§90. If N = p^λ q^μ r^ν s^ξ, then σ(N) = σ(p^λ)σ(q^μ)σ(r^ν)σ(s^ξ). This is full multiplicativity over the prime factorisation, obtained by iterating §86–87 one prime at a time [the iteration is my gloss].

§91. Therefore it suffices to know σ of primes and of prime powers; the latter are geometric sums (p^{n+1}−1)/(p−1), from §84 on the previous page.

§92. Parity remarks:
- For a prime p, σ(p) = p+1 is even except for p=2, where σ(2)=3. Writing an odd prime as p = 2a−1 gives σ(p) = 2a.
- σ(p²) = p²+p+1 is always odd, since p²+p = p(p+1) is even. It can sometimes ('subinde') even be prime: σ(4)=7, σ(9)=13, σ(25)=31.

The chapter as a whole serves to compute σ(n) for all n; this leads to the table of σ(1)…σ(60) and to the remarks on values not attained, on the next page.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page.

§92's 'ac subinde adeo numerus primus' must be read as 'and sometimes even a prime', not 'consequently a prime'. σ(p²) is not always prime: σ(7²) = 57 = 3·19 and σ(11²) = 133 = 7·19. Euler's three examples (7, 13, 31) are correct.
The argument of §86–87 tacitly uses that the sets {d} and {pd} (and {p²d}) are disjoint and exhaust the divisors of Np^k. This holds precisely because p does not divide N, as Euler stipulates.

results.what: σ(Np^k) = σ(N)σ(p^k) for a prime p not dividing N; hence σ(p^λ q^μ …) = ∏σ(p^λ)
results.modern_name: Multiplicativity of the divisor-sum function σ
results.usually_credited_to: Implicit in 17th-c. work on perfect/amicable numbers (Descartes, Wallis); explicitly formulated with notation ∫n by Euler (E175 De numeris amicabilibus, 1750; E243, 1751)

results.what: σ(pⁿ) = 1 + pσ(p^{n−1}) = pⁿ + σ(p^{n−1}), and the iterated forms
results.modern_name: Recursion for the geometric sum σ(pⁿ)
results.usually_credited_to: Elementary; Euler uses it in E243 and the Tractatus

results.what: σ(p) is even for odd primes p; σ(p²) is always odd and sometimes prime
results.modern_name: Parity of σ (σ(n) is odd iff n is a square or twice a square)
results.usually_credited_to: Folklore; the general parity criterion is standard

deep.surprise_reason: This is the standard derivation of the multiplicativity of σ and the prime-power formula. Euler published the same material, with the same ∫ notation, in E175/E243 around 1750. The Tractatus itself has been in print since 1849/1862.
